newsitem.title: INDIA: India budget dodges oil price problem.
newsitem.headline: India budget dodges oil price problem.

text.p: In his 1997/98 budget package India's Finance Minister P. Chidambaram dodged one major question mark hanging over the economy -- how to finance subsidised oil prices?

But Chidambaram's avoidance of the oil issue, and surprising omission of expected cuts in oil import tariffs, left analysts a little surer that when he does act he will move decisively and raise state-controlled refined product prices soon.
They reasoned that inaction on tariffs was a signal he will not defer unpopular price hikes by using budgetary support measures like lower duties to paper over a burgeoning oil bill.
"There was no reduction in customs duties, which could have provided some relief, so the only option is a price hike," said Sanjeev Prasad, an oil analyst at Kotak Securities.

Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia told journalists on Saturday, the day after Chidamabaram delivered his widely praised budget, that the oil pool deficit was a problem but not one that would be met from budget allocations.
"A price increase is the only solution," said Shrivatsa Kumar, an analyst at Jardine Fleming (India) Broking.
When product price rises do come they may be accompanied by a rejig of oil import tariffs, involving a cut in the 27 percent duty on crude imports.
"Any change in duties should probably come later as part of a package with oil price increases," said R.K. Pachouri, director of Tata Energy Research.

India's oil pool deficit -- effectively the amount the government owes oil companies for selling products well below world prices -- will hit 158 billion rupees ($4.4 billion) by the end of March, Petroleum Minister T.R. Balu said.

Indian Oil Corp will be owed between 100 billion and 110 billion rupees, Oil and Natural Gas Corp will be owed around 30 billion, while Hindustan Petroleum Corp Ltd and Bharat Petroleum Corp will be owed some 10 to 12 billion.
The handicap of carrying the cost has forced India's oil companies to borrow heavily.
"The budget has been very silent on the sector. The oil companies will benefit only when the oil pool deficit is brought down," said Sanjeev Patni, analyst at brokerage W.I. Carr.
Chidambaram confined new oil measures to exploration, with an eye to turning around India's declining oil output.
Oil stocks trailed other sectors in the raging bull market that followed Chidamabaram's pro-investment, pro-growth budget, as buyers stood back to see what happens to product prices.
BPCL shares gained three percent on the Bombay bourse on Saturday, HPCL rose 2 percent, ONGC gained 10 percent and IOC fell 0.2 percent, while the BSE top 30 index jumped 5.6 percent.

Analysts reckon the needed price hike could come in the next two weeks or after April. Most expectations centre on a price increase of 15 to 20 percent in diesel -- the product where demand growth is fastest and subsidy spending is highest.

Opinions differ on whether the government will be bold enough to hike the price of kerosene, the fuel used by India's poor for cooking and lighting. The outlay on subsidies for kerosene was 63.5 billion rupees in 1996/97, up from 41.9 billion in 1995/96.
Some analysts said the government could raise kerosene prices 10 percent.

Gasoline is likely to go up by the same amount, although it is already about double the price motorists in the United States pay, they said. Liquid petroleum gas is expected to rise between 10 and 15 percent. $1 = 35.8 rupees
